situation:
You are a young adult who moved out of a parent's home two months ago and started a full-time job. You have come to WILLOW CREEK SAVINGS BANK to open an account, and the teller (judge) has offered to walk through where your money should go.

Your former landlord is holding $700 of your $900 deposit for carpet cleaning and will not release it unless you dispute the charges. Your new lease required a fresh $900 deposit, paid out of savings, so you have $1,200 left and about $150 a month you can set aside.

Your employer matches only what you contribute, dollar for dollar, up to $1,600 a year. Putting $150 a month into the employer match locks that money away until retirement, leaving nothing to replace the $700 the landlord is holding. Putting the same $150 into the bank's savings account at 4.2 percent keeps it reachable but gives up the match, roughly $1,600 a year.

The teller (judge) wants you to compare what the bank's accounts pay after fees, weigh that against what the match is worth, and recommend where the $150 should go. The teller (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:

Business background is the same as the situation above.

You want the participant to compare what the bank's accounts pay after fees, to weigh that against what the employer match is worth, and to recommend where the money should go.

You will begin by greeting the participant and asking to hear their ideas. During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: If this goes wrong, who ends up paying for it?
